title: Heating and cooling homes without burning gas
subtitle: State of the art for domestic heat pumps, boilers and new heating and cooling systems, with a running-cost and CO2 simulator.

whyHard.text: Heat pump efficiency falls as the gap between outdoor air and water temperature grows. Many Italian homes have radiators sized for 60–70 °C water, where a heat pump works much harder than with underfloor heating at 35 °C.

The refrigerant is changing under the installer's feet: the revised F-gas Regulation bans F-gases with GWP above 150 in small monoblock heat pumps from 2027 and removes F-gases from them entirely from 2032; split systems follow by 2035.
The natural replacement, propane (R290), is flammable, so charge limits, siting and installer training become part of the design.
Running cost depends on the ratio between the electricity price and the gas price: with the same efficiency, a high ratio can erase the savings. The simulator below shows the break-even point.
Policy is moving fast: no public incentives for stand-alone fossil fuel boilers since 1 January 2025, and a fossil-boiler phase-out planned by 2040.
Upfront cost is the first wall for households: heat pump equipment often costs two to three times the alternatives, and installation can cost as much again.
Finding someone to do the job: the EU cites a long, complex customer journey, a shortage of installers and long waiting periods among the reasons heat pump sales fell in 2023 and 2024.

In a flat the outdoor unit needs a place: a balcony, a roof or a facade the condominium accepts, with the noise kept away from bedroom windows. EU rules allow outdoor units up to 6 kW a sound power of up to 65 dB(A).

The typical Italian household has a 3 kW electricity contract, sized for lights and appliances. A heat pump, an induction hob and a car charger can push past it, so many households electrifying their heating need a power upgrade and pay a higher fixed charge.

A hot-water cylinder for the heat pump needs roughly the floor space of a fridge; combi boilers made it disappear from Italian homes, so finding that space is often the hardest part of the job in a flat.
The fuel being replaced will get dearer: from 2027 the EU emissions trading system for buildings (ETS2) puts a carbon price on heating fuels.

technologies.name: Air-to-water heat pump
technologies.summary: Extracts heat from outdoor air and delivers it to a water circuit for heating and hot water. The central technology for low-carbon heating.
technologies.why: Mature, mass-produced, 3–5 times more efficient than a gas boiler and growing again in Europe.
limits: Efficiency drops with high flow temperatures (old radiators) and very cold weather
Outdoor unit: space, noise and condominium rules
Higher upfront cost than a boiler

experience.text: Feels different from a boiler: radiators or floors run warm rather than hot for long hours, and rooms stay at an even temperature instead of heating up fast in the morning.
The outdoor unit hums and blows cool air; place it away from bedroom windows and neighbours. EU rules cap the sound power at 65 dB(A) for units up to 6 kW.
Installing it takes a few days and space for a hot-water cylinder; expect a power-contract upgrade in many Italian flats.
Servicing is a yearly check; there is no flue and no combustion.

technologies.name: Monoblock heat pump with natural refrigerant (R290, propane)
technologies.summary: Sealed outdoor unit charged with propane, connected to the house only by water pipes.
technologies.why: The F-gas Regulation bans F-gases with GWP above 150 in monoblock units up to 50 kW from 2027 and all F-gases below 12 kW from 2032: natural refrigerants become the standard.
limits: Flammable refrigerant: charge limits and safety distances
Installers need specific training
Fewer models for very high water temperatures

experience.text: All the refrigerant stays sealed outdoors: only water pipes enter the home, which keeps flammable propane out of the flat.
Can deliver hotter water than older models, which helps when the radiators cannot be changed.

technologies.name: Heat pump paired with rooftop solar PV
technologies.summary: PV production runs the heat pump directly or through thermal storage, cutting the electricity bought from the grid.
technologies.why: Both parts are mature, and Conto Termico 3.0 covers joint installation, but the real saving depends on sizing and on how much heat is needed when the sun shines.
limits: Heating demand peaks in winter, when PV output is lowest
Needs smart control and often a storage tank to shift loads

experience.text: Works best when the heat pump and the hot-water cylinder run around midday: heating and hot water become a way to store solar power for the evening.
In a flat, panels usually mean a shared roof and a condominium agreement or an energy community.

technologies.name: Hybrid system: heat pump plus condensing boiler
technologies.summary: The heat pump covers most of the season; the boiler steps in on the coldest days or for high-temperature radiators.
technologies.why: A practical bridge for existing homes. EU guidance still allows incentives for hybrids when the renewable share is considerable, and Conto Termico 3.0 now admits add-on heat pumps next to an existing boiler.
limits: Two machines to buy and maintain
Still burns gas: the CO2 saving depends on how much heat the heat pump covers

experience.text: A low-risk first step: the boiler stays as a safety net on the coldest days, the heat pump does most of the work, and the radiators stay as they are.
Two machines to service, and the gas contract and its fixed charges stay.

technologies.name: Air-to-air split systems with low-GWP refrigerants
technologies.summary: Room air conditioners that also heat; the refrigerant must move to low-GWP options.
technologies.why: Ubiquitous for cooling and efficient for heating, but small air-to-air splits lose F-gases with GWP above 150 from 2029 and all F-gases by 2035, so the product range is in transition.
limits: No domestic hot water
Comfort and noise depend on the room units

experience.text: Heats and cools a room within minutes; air movement and the indoor unit's noise are noticeable at high fan speed.
An air-to-air unit typically costs USD 3,000–6,000 installed, often the cheapest way to add cooling and part of the heating.
Bathrooms, corridors and kitchens usually stay without a unit and rely on heat from the next room or an electric towel rail.

technologies.name: Elastocaloric (solid-state) heat pumping
technologies.summary: Shape-memory alloys release and absorb heat when stretched and relaxed: heat pumping with no refrigerant gas.
technologies.why: Promising temperature lift among solid-state methods, but still at the prototype stage.
limits: Material fatigue over millions of cycles
Actuators and heat transfer still being engineered

experience.text: Nothing to buy yet: a laboratory technology to watch.

technologies.name: Stand-alone condensing gas boiler
technologies.summary: The efficient end of fossil boilers, recovering heat from flue gases.
technologies.why: No public incentives for stand-alone fossil boilers since 1 January 2025, and a phase-out planned by 2040. Ecodesign rules already require at least 86% seasonal efficiency for boilers up to 70 kW.
limits: Locks in gas use and its CO2 for 15–20 years
Exposed to future gas prices and carbon pricing

experience.text: Familiar and compact, but it only condenses (and reaches its rated efficiency) when the return water is below about 55 °C: turning down the flow temperature often saves gas at no cost.
No longer eligible for Italian tax deductions when installed on its own.

technologies.name: Hydrogen boilers for homes
technologies.summary: Boilers burning hydrogen instead of methane.
technologies.why: A review of 32 independent studies found hydrogen worse than heat pumps on cost, efficiency and resources: heating with it needs about five times more electricity than a heat pump.
limits: Large energy losses producing hydrogen
Grid, safety and supply problems

experience.text: Not available to households: no hydrogen reaches homes, and the evidence points to heat pumps and heat networks instead.

technologies.name: Heat-pump water heaters
technologies.summary: A hot-water cylinder with a small heat pump on top, taking heat from the room or outdoor air.
technologies.why: Uses well under half the electricity of a conventional electric water heater, even in cold climates; an easy first step that does not touch space heating.
limits: Cools the room it stands in; better in a utility room or with ducted air
Needs floor space and a drain for condensate
Slower to reheat than a gas combi

experience.text: Looks like an electric boiler, sounds like a quiet fridge; hot water is stored, so a long family shower routine needs the right size.
Can be timed to run when solar panels produce or electricity is cheap.

technologies.name: Insulation and new windows (fabric first)
technologies.summary: External wall insulation, roof and floor insulation and better windows cut the heat the home needs before choosing the system.
technologies.why: Walls built before 1976 lose about three times more heat per square metre than walls built after 2005; insulating makes any system smaller, cheaper to run and more comfortable, and qualifies for Italian tax deductions.
limits: Disruptive and costly; external insulation of a condominium needs a shared decision
Thermal bridges and ventilation need attention, or mould can follow airtightness

experience.text: The most noticeable change is warmer walls and windows: no cold draught near the glass, less condensation, and rooms that stay warm when the heating stops.
Summer improves too when insulation comes with shading: the home heats up more slowly.

technologies.name: Low-temperature emitters: underfloor heating, larger radiators, fan coils
technologies.summary: Bigger heat-releasing surfaces let the same room be heated with 35–45 °C water instead of 60–70 °C.
technologies.why: Heat pumps and condensing boilers are both more efficient with cooler water; the upfront cost estimates for air-to-water heat pumps already include changes to existing radiator systems.
limits: Underfloor heating in an existing flat means new screed and raised floors
Slow response: underfloor heating suits steady temperatures, not quick boosts

experience.text: Underfloor heating feels like warmth from the ground with no visible radiators; fan coils heat quickly and can also cool and dehumidify, with some fan noise.

technologies.name: Weather compensation and smart controls
technologies.summary: The controller lowers the water temperature on mild days and uses room sensors, instead of running at a fixed setting.
technologies.why: EU energy labelling credits a weather compensator with a room sensor (class VI) with 4 percentage points of seasonal efficiency; it is often a settings change rather than new equipment.
limits: Needs correct set-up by the installer
Gains depend on the emitters being large enough for low water temperatures

experience.text: The radiators feel lukewarm for longer instead of hot for a short time; most people only notice a lower bill.

technologies.name: Mechanical ventilation with heat recovery
technologies.summary: Fans supply fresh air and extract stale air through a heat exchanger that passes most of the warmth to the incoming air.
technologies.why: EU ecodesign rules have required at least 73% heat recovery in two-way residential ventilation units since 2018; in airtight, insulated homes it keeps air fresh without the heat loss of open windows.
limits: Ducts are hard to fit in existing flats; single-room units are a compromise
Filters must be changed, and fans use some electricity

experience.text: Fresh air without opening windows: less noise and pollen from outside, and no cold draught; a faint fan noise if poorly installed.

technologies.name: Shading, night ventilation and fans
technologies.summary: External shutters and blinds, opening windows at night and ceiling or desk fans before air conditioning.
technologies.why: A fan uses roughly 25–150 W against 1,000–1,500 W for a small air conditioner, and good envelope design reduces how much cooling is needed at all.
limits: Not enough during long heatwaves in top-floor or poorly insulated flats
Night ventilation depends on security and outdoor noise

experience.text: Closing external shutters during the sunny hours keeps rooms several degrees cooler; the lab shows the difference on the hottest day.

technologies.name: Ground-source heat pumps
technologies.summary: A heat pump that takes heat from the ground through boreholes or buried pipes, which stay at a steady temperature all year.
technologies.why: Higher and steadier efficiency than air-source units and no outdoor fan, but higher upfront costs, largely for the boreholes or buried pipes; it pays off best in larger buildings, for example shared by a condominium.
limits: Drilling permits and space for boreholes
High upfront cost for a single flat

experience.text: Silent outside, since there is no outdoor unit; the drilling takes a few days and the underground loop outlasts several heat pumps.

technologies.name: Thermal storage and pre-heating
technologies.summary: Storing heat in hot-water tanks, phase-change "heat batteries" or the building's own mass, to heat when power is cheap or solar.
technologies.why: Shifting heating away from the evening peak can be cheaper than reinforcing the grid; electric water heaters with simple controls already provide this flexibility.
limits: Needs time-of-use tariffs or own solar to pay back
Compact heat batteries are still expensive

experience.text: Mostly invisible: the house is a little warmer in the afternoon and the heat pump runs less in the evening.

technologies.name: Wood stoves and open fireplaces as main heating
technologies.summary: Burning logs or pellets in stoves and fireplaces.
technologies.why: Non-industrial combustion, mostly home heating with wood, produced 64% of Italy's fine-particulate pollution in 2023; modern certified pellet stoves are far cleaner than open fireplaces, but cleaner air in cities needs fewer of both.
limits: Local bans on old stoves during smog episodes
Fuel handling and chimney cleaning

experience.text: Cosy radiant heat in one room, but uneven temperatures, daily fuel handling and smoke for the neighbours.

aiAngle.text: Predictive control that heats when electricity is cheap or PV is producing, using the building's thermal mass as storage.
Sizing assistants that estimate heat demand and the best flow temperature from bills, floor plans and climate data.
Fault detection on connected heat pumps: spotting refrigerant leaks or poor settings from operating data.
Materials discovery for solid-state heat pumping and low-GWP refrigerants.
Pre-heating homes at midday when solar power is abundant, so heat pumps do not all switch on at the evening peak: the IEA finds this can be cheaper than reinforcing the grid.
Explaining the choice in plain words: a model that simulates the home (like the lab on this site) plus a language model that answers "why is my bedroom cold?" from the simulation, not from guesses.

stories.title: A 1970s flat in a Milan condominium
stories.situation: Gas combi boiler, radiators sized for hot water, single glazing replaced in the 1990s, middle floor.

points.text: A heat pump on the existing radiators keeps the flat warm most of the winter, but on the coldest days the radiators need hotter water than many units deliver: rooms fall short or an electric back-up heater runs.
Larger radiators, or insulating first, bring the water temperature down and the heat pump's efficiency up.
The outdoor unit and a hot-water cylinder need space and the condominium's agreement; the 3 kW electricity contract may need an upgrade.

stories.title: A top-floor flat in Rome that overheats
stories.situation: Roof above, south-facing living room, no air conditioning.

points.text: Under the roof the flat soaks up summer heat; external shutters and night ventilation cut the hottest hours before any machine.
Air-to-air heat pumps then cool the main rooms and heat them in winter, often for less than a new boiler plus air conditioners.

stories.title: Insulate first, or heat pump first?
stories.situation: A leaky flat built before 1976 with a gas boiler and limited budget.

points.text: Insulation lowers the heat the home needs in every scenario and makes walls and windows warmer, which is what most people notice as comfort.
A heat pump alone cuts CO2 at once but works at high water temperature in a leaky home; the order often depends on which works the condominium can agree on.

stories.title: Renting: what can you change?
stories.situation: No say on the boiler or the walls.

points.text: One degree lower on the thermostat, a night set-back and lower radiator water temperature on a condensing boiler cost nothing.
Closing shutters on summer afternoons and using fans before air conditioning keeps rooms cooler and bills lower.
The Social Climate Fund will support heating upgrades for vulnerable households across the EU from 2026.
